utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Usher, could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, Mr. Margetts, how much time would you still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I hope to be done within half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Buhin. I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you gave at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Margetts will now continue his examination-in-chief. You may proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Buhin. You'll recall that last night when we finished, that we were addressing the issue of the investigation of the events in Grubori. And you'd informed the Court that it had been agreed between you and Romanic that an investigation would take place. And you also informed the Court that Ivica Cetina from the Zadar administration had indicated that he would send a crime team for the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to deal with another exhibit. If we could move into private session to deal with that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session. And the exhibit not to be shown to the public.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, sorry for the interruption. Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. If we could please have displayed on the screen Exhibit D57, and it's page 61 in the Croatian, and page 59 of the English, please. Yes, Mr. Registrar, if we could highlight the bottom portion of that entry for that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Buhin, could you please refer to this entry here. This is the Knin log-book recording the operational activities that took -- that were reported to the Knin police station. And I'd just like you to note there that the date is the 26th of August for this entry, which is entry 193. And there's a reference to bodies having been found in Grubori. And you'll see there's two different entries in the right-hand column relating to the measures to be taken. There's one that is written in a similar manner to the entry on the left and then there's different writing below. Now the first entry as to measures to be taken, refers to the fact that it is contemplated that an on-site investigation would be conducted in the morning of the 27th of August. Is that consistent with your recollection of when that investigation was to take place?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is authentic, and it is not in keeping with my recollection. I was certain that we had learned about this event on the morning of the 27th. However, this shows that the event occurred on the 26th, specifically the afternoon of the 26th. This was immediately recorded, entered into the police station log-book. What we see here is -- was agreed with Chief Cedo Romanic there would be an on-site investigation on the 27th of August. This might as well have been added later on in the day, that evening, perhaps, once it had been ascertained that no such action would be possible on that same day. According to what I remember, the event was reported that morning. However, I think this is a more trustworthy source because this is a written document and it was kept in the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, I invite my learned friends if I'm proceeding in a manner which isn't agreed between the parties or accepted between the parties, but I -- I just -- just to assist you in terms of placing this log-book entry in the chronology of events, there's -- as we have received information, the event took place on the 25th, which we believe was a Friday, and quite clearly this entry in the log-book is the following day, the 26th, which we believe is a Saturday. So is that of any assistance to you? Does that assist you in placing these events, in terms of, you know, when the event occurred, when the information was received by you, and the actions that took place?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I don't think this would be of any assistance to me. It has been a very long time. I see now that I have to go back and change my view, the view that I had held up until yesterday, that the event occurred the same day that all these steps were taken. I do, however, realize now that the report came on the previous day. I don't have such a great head for dates, and I didn't take any notes of my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, if you just look at this entry, the entry -- the person reporting the incident is Mihic. And I understand you had conversations with Mihic about what steps would be taken. Is that correct? And you will see that the time at which this report is made is 1500; it's on the third column from the left there. In other words, 3.00 p.m., 3.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could please move on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, when you asked, is that correct, I saw the witness nodding yes, but that does not appear on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Buhin, when I asked you about your conversations that you had with Mr. Mihic, you nodded. So I'll ask you the question again and if you could give an audible response. And that is that I indicated the person reporting the incident was Milos Mihic, and I asked you: "And I understand you had conversations with Mihic about what steps would be taken. Is that correct?" And could you respond to that question audibly.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on what has been recorded, Milos Mihic was the commander of the police station who was the one who received this report and then passed it along to his own chief, Cedo Romanic. We learned about this at the same time. We got in touch with Mr. Cedo Romanic who was Milos Mihic's superior, so then he imparted whatever instructions still needed imparting at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And just to be clear, did you yourself have conversations with Mr. Mihic at this time about these events.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And now if we could move on, Mr. Registrar, please. It's the same document, but if we could move forward to page 63 in the Croatian and that is page 61 of the English. And the entry that I'm interested in is entry number 197, which is the second one down, Mr. Registrar. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Buhin, could I direct your attention to the second entry. It's again in the Knin daily log of events held at the police station, and this time it refers to an entry that was reported by a Mr. Karolj Dondo. Can you inform the Trial Chamber as to who Mr. Dondo was?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And you'll see in this entry, again it refers to events in Grubori but this time this entry is made at 2000, which is five hours after the other entry. It describes the events as being the finding of five bodies who were killed during military and police Operation Storm. Now, at that stage, in the evening of the 26th of August, did you have any knowledge about a military and police operation having been conducted in the area of the Grubori village; that is the Plavno valley area.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I had no information indicating that. However, if I may just comment on the entry. The shift had changed. There was a changing of the shift at 1900 hours. Some people stayed and some people left. The duty officer entered this information. I'm not sure to what extent he was familiar with the substance. Nevertheless, the established practice was for everything, all reports to be recorded. So that's what he did. We often had different reports on the same developments, so this was the case in point. There was this policeman who came to the station to tell us about the bodies. The entry should be reflected literally in the same way or the report should be reflected literally in the same way that it was delivered, and I believe that was the case here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, there is a significant difference in this entry to the previous entry, apart from the number of bodies which we've already noted. But in the measures taken or the action that is proposed, in this entry, there is no reference to an investigation. In fact, the officer wrote that the information will be passed on to civilian protection officers for hygiene and sanitation. Now, this is at 8.00 p.m. on the 26th of August. Now, at that stage, were you aware of any decision having been taken that there should be a change from what's recorded at 3.00 p.m., and in fact, instead of the investigation, there should be sanitation of the terrain?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is probably an omission on the part of the police station commander who was supposed to go through the entries each morning. At the time, I don't know who was on duty and in charge at the police station. Having followed the situation as it developed at the time, as soon as the report came in about the bodies being found following combat, the civil protection people would be informed. They had a forensic person who would go to a scene immediately and then this sanitation would take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Buhin, that -- that's helpful information that you are providing. It's just that my question was little more specific and it was a question as to whether you were aware that -- of any change in circumstances between 3.00 p.m. and 8.00 p.m. on the 26th of August, that instead of investigation there should be sanitation of the bodies in Grubori. Were you made aware of any one --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- matter of accuracy here which may be important given the witness's last answer. He never said "instead."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That could be clarified then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I don't entirely follow Mr. Kay's suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think that Mr. Kay does not -- let's -- I could clarify that. Mr. Buhin, when was it decided, if this was decided, that no investigation team would be sent to Grubori? When did you become aware?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That -- I found out that an investigation team had not attended the scene, only several days later. And the agreement was in the morning, when I and my colleague Ivo Baric were at the UNPROFOR police headquarters, that the scene would be attended after two to three hours, once we had set up a team from Zadar. All day, until sometime in the afternoon, there was every indication that the on-site investigation would indeed be conducted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you then tell us this conversation with Mr. Sacic, which is described in your statement, when that took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was sometime around midday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On what day? 27th, 26th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 27th, sometime around 1200 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, from your statement I read that it was explained to you that -- no, that you told him that you had taken steps and that an investigation would take place and that Mr. Sacic became angry and said that you -- that you -- that the bodies would be processed and clearly contradicting your plans to have the investigation, as you had on your mind. Now, you tell us that only a couple of days after that you learned that no investigation with the investigation -- investigating judge had taken place. Is that how I have to understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, you understand me properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And when Mr. Sacic told you that what you intended was not what should happen, did you get any impression that the investigation would be -- not take place; or did you still consider for a couple of days that the investigation, as it was planned by you and as it was agreed that should take place, that that would take place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believed that the investigation would take place in the afternoon on that same day, the same day when the investigative judge's team from Zadar was formed and when the team of on-site investigation experts, crime scene examiners, was set up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what Mr. Sacic said raised no doubt in your mind as to whether such an investigation would take place at all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never doubted it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me try to understand. You agreed that an investigation with a investigating judge will take place. Then Mr. Sacic comes, apparently there was some communication with Mr. Moric as well, and Mr. Sacic says, No way, you do it totally wrong. This is not what should happen. And then you still expected that things would go on as you had in mind and not as Mr. Sacic had -- apparently on his mind. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That I believed the on-site investigation would certainly take place. And after Mr. Moric had called me on the telephone, some 15 minutes or so, after my conversation with Mr. Sacic, Mr. Moric, quite angrily told me that I should not actually do the job of the crime police but that I should do the job for which I had been assigned to Zadar, which were duties of public order and traffic. After that, I no longer was concerned with the on-site investigation and the crime police duties but continued doing my other tasks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Buhin, just to be clear on this, as you recalled and you've related to the Trial Chamber, the information about this event reached you, as you understood it, in -- on a morning, during a morning, and did you consider that the investigation would take place that same day?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And as you understand it, was that the same day that you met with Mr. Sacic or a day prior to your meeting with Mr. Sacic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the same day after we had the conversation with the UN police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes. And did that conversation with the UN police take place on the -- well, on the day prior to your meeting with Mr. Sacic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could now move into private session again, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Buhin, you referred in your statement to the fact that during Operation Flash and those times that you received maps from the special police that indicated to you where any operations would take place. And I'm just interested to know, in terms of your desire to locate the village of Grubori, did either you or Mr. Baric, or Mr. Romanic, or perhaps Mr. Mihic or anyone you know of, make inquiries with any of the special police or military command as to whether they would be able to assist you with maps of the location of the Plavno valley?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is probably a mistake on the part of us all, that was a mistake on the part of us all because no one got in touch with special police officers after -- after having learned of these events. And that is why Mr. Sacic was angry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Buhin. That concludes my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And thank you, Mr. President, that concludes the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Margetts. Could I ask you one question to clarify the last answer you gave. You said no one got in touch with special police officers and that Mr. Sacic was angry. Did he expect you to have got in touch with the special police on the matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know who -- whom he expected to do that, but we did not have any direct contacts with special police officers there during our stay there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you have -- did you gain any impression on whether the special police would or should play a role in revealing what had happened in Grubori? Were they to play a role?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that they were to play a role, in view of the fact that Mr. Sacic said that the special police had a mopping up action in that area. Now, that area could be a broader term. I cannot be very specific in that particular sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To your knowledge, were they still in the area or would they return to that area? And I'm talking about the area of Grubori.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Throughout my stay in the area of Knin, I had no information whatsoever about the activities of the special police, in terms of where they were, what area they were in, and similar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were you informed whether they would be sent to further investigate or further -- make further findings on the situation in Grubori?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. After talking with Mr. Moric, I was no longer concerned with that segment of the assignment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did he tell you whether the special police would be sent to the area but now for the purpose of clarifying or investigating or revealing what -- or make any findings on what had happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Ours was a very short conversation. He only angrily told me not to butt in the work of the crime police but to do my assigned job. That was the long and the short of our conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And no one else told that you the special police would be sent there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. Who will be the first one to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour, on behalf of Mr. Cermak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Buhin, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Kay. Mr. Kay is counsel for Mr. Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Buhin, I want to ask you some questions, first of all, about your briefing by Mr. Moric and Mr. Djurica before you went down to Knin. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You told us that you had a briefing by those two superiors to you. Whereabouts was that briefing?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in one of the offices. I'm not sure whether it was Mr. Moric's or Mr. Djurica's office, but it was on the premises of the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So that would be in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. In the Ministry of the Interior, in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And which day was that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it was the 5th of August, the same day when the army entered Knin. After we had learned from the mass media that the army had entered Knin, we were called to either Mr. Moric's or Mr. Djurica's office; I'm not sure at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And so did you arrive in Knin on the next day, the 6th of August?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At the briefing by Mr. Moric and Mr. Djurica, what matters did they brief you about?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a very short briefing. They confirmed to us what we had already heard from the mass media, namely, that Croatian troops had entered Knin. And that we were chosen individually, by name, to be assigned as coordinators to the just liberated area. I and Mr. Baric were assigned to the police administration and the police station in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was your role as a coordinator defined for you?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not much was said at that point about it. We were just told that we were to help with the organisation and functioning of the police administration and the police station, in terms of law and order and safe traffic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Had you operated in a similar role as a coordinator before?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was it a position that you were able to understand what you had to do after Mr. Moric and Mr. Djurica had briefed you?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, yes. Yes, we understood our task that we were to assist the new leadership, the chief of the police administration, the chief of the police station to find their bearings and for the police station and the police administration to start functioning, conducting the basic duties of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And was it one of the purposes for this role that because you came from Zagreb and the police administration, that you would be able to help Mr. Romanic in setting up the Kotar-Knin police administration on the ground?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was our objective, to help organise that administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Before this day of the 5th of August, had you been aware of joint steps taken by Mr. Moric on behalf of the Ministry of Interior with the military police administration, in cooperation and coordination between the two police forces during Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were not aware, not I and not my colleagues, about any preparations for Operation Storm, until the moment that we were called for that short briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At that stage, did you learn, or subsequently learn, about the steps of cooperation between the MUP and the military police?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean measures during Operation Oluja, or customary measures, steps?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Measures to be taken after Operation Oluja.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At that time, I was not aware of any meetings or of any agreements to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you arrived in Knin on the 6th of August, had you been to Knin before?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And can you recollect at what time of day you arrived in Knin?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was sometime around midday. We came from the police administration in Zadar and were being led by police officer in the direction of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was that the day that the minister of interior, Mr. Jarnjak, opened the police station in Knin?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The minister never came to Knin during my stay there. It was only after two or three days that Mr. Moric arrived for five minutes or so, only just to put up the plaque on the police station, and he left immediately after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So you were there when the plaque was put on the police station.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was there. The plaque was put there on -- on the second or third day, after I had arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And when you arrived at the police station in Knin, what state did you find the building in?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of the police administration, Cedo Romanic, and a couple of policemen were already in the building. The building was quite ransacked, and there were two shell holes inside. The entire place had been ransacked and it was hard to find one's way about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And did you help Mr. Romanic to start, establish a working police station from that building?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the extent that we could. To the extent that we were able to give him a hand at that time. There were no links to the Zadar police administration; that's one thing we must bear in mind, and no links to the ministry either. The policemen were new in the area as well. They had arrived from other areas and were not familiar with Knin or indeed its surroundings. We did our best to, little by little, take over police affairs in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your headwear is being adjusted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the best way to take care that it doesn't fall off is to have the band on top of your head rather than ... like --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: All right? How long did it take to establish Knin police station as a -- a working police station?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: After two or three days, we started doing all the basic things. Duty rotation, recording daily events, and we started drawing up schedules, work schedules, on day one, in terms of which officers would be dispatched to which area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And was that work that you were helping Mr. Romanic with?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was more Mr. Mihic that we were helping, who, at the time, was chief or commander, I'm not sure what the term was at the time, of the Knin police station. As for Mr. Romanic, we helped him try to link up all the police stations in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We know that Kotar-Knin police administration relied on Zadar-Knin police station for support. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All of the support and assistance came through the Zadar police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And how long was it before you had links with Zadar-Knin police administration?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on the kind of work involved. For the first five to eight days, we had no water, no electricity, no radio communications. We would try to distribute information and spread information to the extent that we could and were trying to gradually bring life back to normal. But the station had not yet reached its full capacity, not even by day 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was it difficult working conditions to establish an effective police administration in those circumstances?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conditions were exceptionally difficult. We didn't have the equipment, we didn't have enough money, nor indeed did we have a sufficient number of trained people who were properly trained to perform those kinds of operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At the beginning, how many police officers did you have working for Kotar-Knin police administration and the Knin police station?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you a figure. But there were probably about 50 police officers from Split-Dalmatia police administration and about the same amount from Zadar. Very few, you might say. We had used up a lot of our manpower trying to secure some important facilities and features such as sources of water, the Orthodox monastery at Kistanje where we set up a police outpost, and there was a factory there too. There were a number of other features in addition to our own place station. There was some facilities for police accommodation and all of that needed securing. We also had to set up a number of check-points throughout the area. We did not have sufficient manpower. It wasn't before the end of that month that another contingent of about 50 men was sent over to us from Krapina-Zagorje police administration. By this time, we had already stepped up traffic control and other such routine operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We know that Kotar-Knin police administration had eight police stations underneath it, and the Kotar-Knin police administration was the supporting administration for those fundamental police stations on the ground. What about the manpower, the police officers, to take up position within those other police stations within the region? How soon were you able to achieve that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: These forces were being deployed by the Ministry of Interior in Zagreb and this was done from Zagreb. They dispatched police officers directly to certain police stations. I believe that as soon as the 6th, all of the police officers who were meant to be dispatched were already at their respective police stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And how many policemen were there at these other police stations in the region?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact figures, and I don't think it would be a good idea for me to just round it off.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What was your relationship, how did you work with those other police stations outside Knin?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Over the first two or three weeks, communication would occur no more than once a week at meetings organised by Mr. Franjo Djurica, who was the coordinator in charge of these newly liberated areas. He provided a link between us and the ministry. He would always schedule meetings and each time this would occur at a different police station, and then all the chiefs and police station commander, chiefs of police administrations would meet, problems would be raised, and assignments agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And were those meetings that you would go to?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the matters discussed at those meetings with Mr. Djurica and the other police commanders were what kind of matters? What was discussed on a weekly basis between the commanders of the police stations and Mr. Djurica?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, each of the station commanders spoke about their own prospective areas and the problems they were encountering. At the outset, there was a serious problem involving numerous persons wearing Croatian army uniforms freely roaming about the area, committing all sorts of offences and crimes. There were cases of arson, looting, and so on. There were even some murders. So that was the main subject that we covered. There was also the question of putting up all these police officers somewhere in the area, the conditions under which they worked, and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And what was Mr. Djurica's reaction when he heard about these kinds of problems being told to him by the commanders of the police stations?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the roughest of terms, the reactions were, We'll try to improve our cooperation with the military police. Do what you can within your powers. He would also inform the ministry about our problems, expecting that they would provide some sort of assistance. There was a general shortage of police officers throughout all these areas, in terms of sufficient numbers. That's what I'm saying. Little by little things were, however, improving, and circumstances, more and more, started favouring us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You referred to the problem of people in uniform committing offences. Was it difficult to find out whether those were civilian people in military uniform or whether they were genuine-serving military personnel?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was very difficult. There were a few police teams patrolling the area. Police officers and police vehicles are easy to spot from a distance. So whenever there was a police presence in an area, no such incidents would occur. It wasn't before one actually got to talk with locals in these areas that we were able to find out that persons were spotted roaming about wearing Croatian army uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Given the circumstances that you had entered into in this liberated region, did you have any of the usual police techniques for monitoring law and order available to you? By that, I mean established intelligence links, information coming from various sources. Did you have anything like that established to help you deal with law and order?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I have pointed out already, it was very difficult. There was no proper radio communication because we didn't have the repeaters required for that sort of communication. For the first eight days, there was no electricity in the broader Knin area. The direct approach was the only course of action. Police officers would have to go to and fro. They would have to go back to the station to bring reports. They would have to go out and check reports. These police officers were now in an area that was unfamiliar and they were scared, scared of enemy fire, scared of booby-traps. So for the first 15 to 20 days, the working conditions were exceptionally difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'd just like to look at a document to see whether it's one that you recognise or whether you can comment upon it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we have Exhibit D600, please, on the screen. This is a document dated the 6th of August, 1995, and it was sent to the police administrations by Mr. Zidovec, and amongst the police administrations were Zadar-Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we look at the document, first of all, it concerns records of fires and wanting statistical records about fires and giving the reason, the result of combat operations in the areas of your police administrations. And information was to be sent to the headquarters giving matters that would help the statistics. First of all, was this a document that you saw when you arrived as a coordinator down in Knin?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see this document. For the first few days, no mail arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We know it was sent to Zadar-Knin, and we know that the Kotar-Knin police administration was established the day before, on the 5th of August, 1995. Was there a problem in having communication sent to the Kotar-Knin police administration?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were problems. We received all documents such as this one, or orders, with a one or two-day delay. For example, when one of our messengers went to Zadar or when a messenger arrived Knin from Zadar, we would probably receive something like this on day two or day three. I don't remember this document as such. I do know, however, that we recorded all of our incoming mail. As soon as the communications were up and running, we informed the ministry directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's just look at another document, D43, Exhibit D43. This is dated the 7th of August, 1995, and it's to the police administration of Split-Dalmatia, operations staff. Again, from Mr. Zidovec and it concerns assistance to the Zadar-Knin police administration --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, could I just go back to the previous document for one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you explained to us that mail would be received with a delay of one or two days. Could we just go back to the previous document and have a look at the stamp at the bottom of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: While we're doing that, can I tell Your Honour that it doesn't go to the Kotar-Knin police administration; it goes to the Zadar-Knin police administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Therefore I'm seeking clarification on who received what, where, at what time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because it is not entirely clear, also on the bottom, who received it. It was received on the same day apparently by someone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I wanted to ask the witness whether he could give us further clarification on what that stamp exactly tells us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you have a look at the stamp at the bottom? If it could be enlarged. And could we also have the English, the -- if possible, the entirety of the document --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, it's on the bottom of the first page, apparently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Ah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us who signed or -- I see a number, 47, shift leader. Could you tell us, could you give us a clue as to who signed for the receipt of this document with this stamp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say. The shift leader, probably. This was the operations duty of the police administration and it could have been any of these police administrations cited above.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, looking at the time, it's an hour and a half since we started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if this would be a suitable moment for you. Perhaps we first ask Mr. Usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which gives me an opportunity to inquire with the parties on timing. Mr. Kay, since you are the first one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, three and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Three and a half hours. Still to go or in total?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I can't remember when I started, Your Honour, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Approximately half an hour ago, from what is my recollection, because Mr. Margetts indicated at five minutes past 3.00, I think it was, that my conception of half an hour should be adjusted and he had one question remaining.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that accords with my memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you are a little bit over half an hour, Mr. Kay. Another three hours or another three and a half hours?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Another three and a half hours, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will be the second one, Your Honour. And, of course, it depends on Mr. Kay's progress. I'll assume that I wouldn't take more than an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I don't expect to be more than an hour, and, again, I anticipate probably less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Altogether we have six hours still to go. Isn't it true that a videolink has been prepared for tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I get an impression on how much time the videolink would take because it is very difficult to cancel a videolink.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is my understanding in discussions with the Defence that the cross-examination will, all in likelihood, certainly be less than an hour total for all three teams.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Less than an hour total.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, we would be only half an hour in chief with the videolink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if we would work efficiently, in one session with the videolink. Let me ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What we then should try to achieve is to hear the testimony of this witness today and tomorrow, apart from the first session tomorrow in which we would have a videolink, which would mean that we have four sessions remaining, which should do for the six hours. If Defence could try to be as efficient as possible, then there's a chance perhaps, Mr. Margetts, that any re-examination needed could be done. I don't know whether there would be many questions of the witness, but let's try to see whether we can finish both this witness and the videolink witness by the end -- by the close of business of tomorrow. If everyone keeps that on his mind, then we will have a break until quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm going to change the document that we were going to look at in the interests of speed. Can we look at Exhibit D583, please. This is letter dated the 8th of August, 1995, from Mr. Moric and sent to all the police administration chiefs, referring to a telegram that he'd sent on the 4th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And I'd like you to look at this document, please, Mr. Buhin, as it refers to heightened security measures, which you referred to as being problems for the police. We can see this document from Mr. Moric, and ordering increased coverage of places and features that could be the subject of a terrorist attack, and despite measures we saw attempts of attack against transport, vital industrial facilities by terrorist laying large amounts of explosives, and referring to future attacks by sabotage and terrorist attacks. So he orders to assiduously cover vital transport infrastructure, strengthen security of features of significance and strengthen security of features and infrastructure in the ownership of the police administration. That is Mr. Moric's order, Mr. Buhin. It was sent to all police administration chiefs. Did you receive this document through the system?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember specifically this document but I probably did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The matter that the document is dealing with concerning terrorist attacks and sabotage, were they matters that you had to deal with in relation to the use of the police?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they certainly were. This the period immediately following the Operation Oluja, when terrorist attacks were to be expected, and everyone in his respective area had to make a security assessment in terms of what facilities might come under attack and how to protect them. This is what we did, too. That is why we posted security around the Orthodox monastery because it was to be expected that it might come under attack and be demolished. Then also the water catchment point, which is also a facility of vital importance, was guarded, as were some bridges and factories. There was also a military proving ground which was used by Milan Martic's special police forces. There were also other facilities. I cannot recall them all at this point, but we posted quite a few of our forces to such guard posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So the role of the police at this stage in Knin, would it be right to say, faced three tasks: Ordinary police work, as one task; establishing the police station and the police system as another task; as well as dealing with potential conflict that there may be against the state.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those were the fundamental -- these are the fundamental tasks of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you arrived in Knin, you had met Mr. Moric and Mr. Djurica at that stage. How often did Mr. Moric come down to the Knin region to see what was happening?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He only came once, when he brought the plaque with the inscription "police station" and "police administration," and he only stayed for five minutes or so on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we look at the Exhibit P962, which was the organigram you looked at yesterday. And that organigram detailed the tasks of senior police officers as well as showing where they fitted in to the Ministry of Interior structure. You told us about Mr. Djurica coming down for weekly meetings with the police commanders. Did he come down to Knin more frequently than that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is difficult for me to be sure, but he did come between those meetings, to talk to just us, in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And what would be he talking to you about when he came down to Knin?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conversation was always about the current problems that we were grappling with. It depended on the actual time when he came and what problems we had at that specific moment, and we tried to deal with them together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So, broadly, would those problems he was discussing with you, concern people committing crimes?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the problems concerned more the fundamental duties of the police, and we actually diverted the problems dealing with the commission of crimes to the criminal police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So if we look at our organigram here, Exhibit P962, we see that Mr. Benko was the assistant minister in charge of the crime police. How often did he go down to Knin, if you're able to say?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall him coming to Knin at all while I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We see on the organigram that Mr. Nadj is the chief of the crime police sector, beneath Mr. Benko. Were you aware of him coming down to Knin region, not necessarily just the town but the Knin region.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember him coming either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You've told us about Mr. Kardum, who was the chief of the Zadar-Knin crime police. Did he come to Knin and have meetings and discuss problems?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that he did come, but I cannot recall a specific instance. I know him from that time. Actually, I met him for the first time while I stayed in Knin. But I'm not sure whether he came directly to Knin, whether we had in encounter in Knin or in Zadar. Much time has elapsed, so I cannot be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Cetina, who was chief of the Zadar-Knin police administration, did you meet him in Knin or elsewhere to discuss problems with the policing of the region?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Cetina did come. He came on different occasions to Zadar [as interpreted], and we discussed both police work and civilian protection duties because he was in charge of both.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And at these meetings, were people like Mr. Cetina and Mr. Djurica trying to give you support for your work as -- or for the work of the Kotar-Knin police administration?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had the feeling that they did their utmost to the best of their ability, to help us. But then again their own abilities were restricted in terms of securing the necessary equipment for us, and the necessary number of police officers, so that most of it was just confined to us stating our problems and then them seeking to help us to alleviate or overcome those problems, but they certainly did assist us to the best of their ability.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. Just at line 38, 1, there's a reference to Zadar and in light of the question, and the -- the start of the answer at -- I think 25 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think the witness -- it is my recollection that the witness said something different. Could you please -- when you said, Mr. Cetina did come, he came on different occasions to where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm grateful to Mr. Margetts. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So as you said, you were working with the fundamental police. That's the ordinary police. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The crime police who investigated crimes were separate from your responsibility. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you able to judge whether there was enough crime police to support you in your work when you reported crimes to the Zadar-Knin police administration?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I remember that a constant problem was the number of equipped teams for on-site investigations and of crime inspectors because the same number of people had to cover, over a very short period of time, a much larger area than before, whereas their number had not been increased. On the other hand, criminal offences were also on the rise, considerably.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you aware also of measures taken by the Ministry of Interior, the MUP, to cooperate and coordinate with the military police, to establish a -- a system of law and order and control right at the start of Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in meetings with Mr. Franjo Djurica, we were always instructed to try and maintain as good as a cooperation as possible with the military police, that we should exchange information on events and incidents and seek to establish jointly manned check-points, which were actually established some 15 or 20 days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you meet and have discussions with Major Juric, who was the commander of the 72nd and 73rd Military Police Battalions in the region from the 2nd of August, in fact, 1995, until the 13th of August, 1995? Did you meet him?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not as a rule, because colleague Ivo Baric assumed that duty of meeting with Mr. Cermak and also with the military police people, together with Cedo Romanic. I do remember that this person, this gentleman came, if we are talking about the same person, to our offices at the police administration. Someone from the police administration did come. Whether it was specifically that gentleman, I'm not sure, because I do not know him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: He would have been from the military police administration. Do you mean someone came from the military police administration?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Someone, one of the officers of the military police came on several occasions to our offices, in order for us to agree on exchanging information, on joint actions and so on and so forth, but I do not recall the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you aware of various orders that were issued by Mr. Moric to the police administrations, telling them to cooperate with the military police?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the orders issued by Mr. Moric also reached us at Knin so that I had to be aware of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You told us that you arrived in Knin on the 6th of August.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you receive orders that had been issued by Mr. Moric, by the chief of military police administration, before that date, so that you knew what had been decided between the MUP, on the one hand, and the military police administration on the other hand, as to how they were going to work together?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first days of my stay in Knin, I did not see any such orders. It was probably only after contacts with Mr. Franjo Djurica that we, the coordinators, were also informed of these tasks and of these instructions, i.e., orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So from what you could tell, had Mr. Djurica been in contact with the military police administration as to how you were going to work jointly with them?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that, but he probably had been. I only don't know at what command level of the military police that contact was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: From what you say, it was Mr. Baric who was the other coordinator who worked with the military police. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you and he separate your roles as to the kind of tasks that you would do?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had agreement to the effect that I should see more to the fundamental police work in the station and also deal with some matters associated with administration; and he was to work with the army and the military police more, but we did share the workload.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So when you established your police check-points in the Knin region, did you do that, or did he establish the check-points? Or did you both work together?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, we did that work jointly, and the check-points were set up immediately after our arrival.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How did you select those places that you set the check-points at?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We used a map. We used the map that we had found in the building, and we freely assessed what directions would be the most interesting from our standpoint. The busiest roads, that is to say, were the ones that we established check-points at, although there was not much traffic to speak of at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And as you learnt more about the area, did you move your check-point positions?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were not constant. We wanted to set them up near overpasses, bridges, where there were facilities which required protection and supervision, and roads where we expected busier traffic where there would be vehicles and people passing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You were referred to the joint check-points you had with the military police yesterday. Did you establish your check-points first and they then join you at the check-points, so that they became joint check-points?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first, we had separate check-points. But the military police also had their own check-points from the very first days, where they controlled and supervised the passage of persons wearing military uniforms, the passing of military vehicles and so on, and we controlled the passage of civilian vehicles and persons. But they also had their check-points. Initially they were separated, but upon some insistence, they were later joined.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I just want to look at the joint check-points. You referred to them having a separate check-point. Do you mean by that that they were in the same place but 20 metres or even 30 metres apart from where the fundamental police had their check-point?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As a rule, we covered the same roads. Distances varying depending on the lie of the land between the two, 20, 30, or even 10 metres, in some cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And was one of the reasons for that that it made sense to filter the military police into dealing with the military; and you to have a filter dealing with civilians, so that the task became easier to divide the two separate groups?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: However, did it then change so that you started to work not separately but as mixed check-points, where you would both be together at the same point?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we could just look at Exhibit D49, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 18th of August. And it was sent by Mr. Moric to the police administrations, including Knin, and concerns crimes being committed, and also individuals who are not members of the Croatian army but are wrongfully wearing Croatian army uniforms, as well as individuals who are formally and actually members of the Croatian army. And then he made an order. And we can see at paragraph 3 he refers to mixed check-points and mixed patrols, as well as, in 4, he refers to on-site investigations that would be conducted after every case of torching and illegal taking away of property as of today. Do you remember receiving this order from -- from Mr. Moric, which was sent to the Knin police administration?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember specifically receiving this document. I do, however, believe that I received it and that the document was followed through.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Would it be the sort of matter that Mr. Djurica was discussing with the police commanders when he came to the region?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In your work that you were trying to do, were you attempting to stop criminal offences being committed?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was certainly the case. To the extent that it was possible, under the circumstances. We had very few available police officers. When I say available, I mean not manning any check-points or securing any facilities or features in the area. We would, as a matter of fact, send out patrols to areas in which crimes were occurring, such as looting and arson. Whenever there were police officers patrolling an area, as a rule, nothing would happen. But even so, just by dispatching officers to an area we already achieved something, as a rule. It's difficult to say whether in this way we actually managed to forestall or prevent any crimes from happening, but that's what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And how closely did you supervise your police officers who were working for you?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We toured police-manned check-points on an almost daily basis. One of us, one of the coordinators, perhaps Mr. Baric, normally with the chief of the police administration, Mr. Romanic or the commander of the police station, we would go out and tour the check-points to make sure for ourselves whether they were manning the points that they were supposed to be manning, whether they were carrying out their assignments as ordered and what sort of problems they were encountering. So yes, we did check regularly. As for police teams being dispatched to certain areas, they were impossible to keep under control in the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Point 4 of the document we've just looked at, which refers to "on-site investigations and forensic and operative criminal processing will be conducted after every case of torching ... houses and illegal taking away of people's movable property," were you aware if on-site investigations were not being conducted in relation to these sorts of crimes before the 18th of August?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, prior to this order, such incidents were just recorded in our logs and then there would be numerical accounts of these incidents that would, in due course, be forwarded to the Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In what circumstances would you conduct -- contact the crime police in Zadar-Knin?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever the assistance of the crime police was required or whenever they had to go an area to carry out an on-site investigation, depending very much on the situation. And then someone would be informed in the Zadar police administration. Sometimes this would be done by Mr. Romanic directly; sometimes it would be the duty officers of the police station. Once they'd got their system set up a little, they would send operative reports to the Zadar police administration, depending on the incident and depending on the channel that was used to forward this type of information. This, of course, was the case whenever a crime occurred and whenever an on-site investigation was required.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you able to contact Zadar-Knin right from the start to ask them to carry out on-site investigations, if a crime was recorded or reported to you?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I say, in the first days it was very difficult to communicate and it was slow going because we needed to dispatch a messenger to Zadar to take our messages there, and the same thing applied the other way around. Nonetheless, when the presence of the crime police was required, information would always be sent through to them eventually. The only matter here was the time-lag between this and the time we found out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we look at Exhibit D584, please. This a document dated 19th of August, 1995, from Mr. Cetina, the chief of the Zadar-Knin police administration, and it concerns the previous document we've just looked at. And he refers to a meeting on the 16th of August, with the deputy commander of the 72nd Battalion of the military police, Mr. Primorac, which was held on that day. And on the 17th of August, 1995, a meeting with the commander of the 71st Battalion of military police, Mr. Matanic. And both those men pointed out that "coordinated action at all check-points was impossible due to lack of personnel."

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: First of all, were you aware of any contacts that Mr. Cetina had with the military police concerning joint work with the ordinary police?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In some way, yes. I certainly was informed about that directly through Mr. Cetina or perhaps following Mr. Baric's meetings with officers of the military police or perhaps following meetings with General Cermak. At any rate, I must have known about that in the meetings in one way or another. It's difficult for me to pinpoint this exactly, as it has been a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was that a problem that you were aware of, that there were insufficient numbers of military police to do some of the tasks required of them?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm positive that that was one of the major problems. There was a problem involving uniformed police and I believe the same applied to the military police. They were unable to cover all the requirements. I don't know about the numbers of men the military police had available to them at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You referred to the meetings that took place. In relation to meetings with General Cermak, it's right that you, yourself, didn't attend any of those meetings.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never even met General Cermak in person. I knew that he was around, but we simply never happened to be in the same room. As simple as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And did you know what his job was in Knin?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you what my understanding was at the time and, as a matter of fact, it still is. His role was to bring together the civilian authorities, the civilian police, the role of the army in the area. His role was that of coordination. He was supposed to link up all these different activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And was that why there were these meetings at garrison command?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so. He, too, had to know what was going on and he had to know everything that the police knew about and all the steps taken by the police. In addition to police work like that, I believe he had to monitor everything else that was going on. Therefore, the meetings were necessary, even on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And was this because of the circumstances of Knin having been liberated and was not a fully functioning or normally functioning town?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. There wasn't a single body that could do its work properly at the time. We were warming up, getting into our stride, as it were. And the same applied to the civilian authorities, the medical bodies that were operating in the area. So the problems faced over those first couple of days were great, and what this required was someone linking up all these different fields of activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did it make sense to you, then, to have all these different agencies meeting to discuss problems?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it did. This was the only way we could get ourselves up and running. This was the only way we could start doing something in terms of exchanging information, see what the other people were having to deal with and how it -- how they were going about resolving any difficulty or problems that they were facing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: For instance, opening of shops or banks. Was that the kind of information that would be important for you to know, if that was happening in Knin town?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most certainly. We, too, had to keep a close watch on such facilities and features in order to prevent any looting or robbery. It was only to be expected that such institutions and facilities would be at a risk.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And from what you say about meetings, is it right that the fundamental police, through Mr. Baric or through Mr. Romanic, had separate meetings with the military police outside of meetings at General Cermak's office?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were several meetings on the military police premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And were you aware of meetings taking place at a higher level, where Mr. Moric from the Ministry of Interior, General Lausic from the military police administration and other senior MUP and military police personnel, were meeting to discuss problems that they both faced in the liberated areas?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were informed about such meetings at our own meetings with Mr. Djurica or directly by Mr. Moric, who would send us written notes about such meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The problems that other agencies faced within the town and region of Knin, were they reported to you; for instance, the problems in getting the normalization of life to the town?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes we would learn about these problems in other secondary ways. But we didn't look into our people's business that much because we each dealt with our own business within our own respective systems. So, yes, we were aware of problems faced by the health bodies or institutions. We would get reports from further afield or we would ourselves sometimes drive people to hospitals to collection or reception centres. People were hungry and thirsty. We would go on to inform civilian authorities about these situations, the social welfare office or Mr. Pasic, or Pasalic's office, or whatever his name was. There were steps that were taken, but this wasn't really our line of work or our concern in the strictest sense of the word.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In terms of the military hierarchy, the structure of the military, do you know about that, how the military was structured, about the ranks and positions within the military of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't busy myself thinking about that at the time. Even now, I'm still unable to really distinguish.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Have you ever served in the military?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Back in 1972. That was my regular military term with the JNA. The conditions had changed, obviously, after the breakup of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let's turn to 1995. Did you know what position within the Croatian military General Cermak had?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, he was a general. I'm not sure which unit he commanded. I do know that he was a commander in the Knin area. But which unit, how many men, I was never privy to that type of detail about the Croatian army, and I never looked hard, if you see what I mean. I know that he was the commander in chief in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In terms of his actual position, did you know what that was, what his position within the Split Military District was?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And in your statement, you say: "In my opinion, General Cermak was in charge of the military." Do you think you had enough knowledge to give an opinion such as that? Did you know enough about the military to give your opinion as to whether he was in charge of the military?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not then, not now, as I explained a minute ago. I wasn't familiar with the military structure or hierarchy of the Croatian army. When I stated that, I knew that he was the main commander for the army, which is really a very broad notion, but I did not know anything more specific than that about his powers or about his specific units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And in relation to any area of responsibility, did you know anything about that, what his area of responsibility was?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the newly liberated territory or what used to be known as Kotar-Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And did you have any document or information about that that told you that, or is it a guess?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a guess. I had no information available to me, orally or written.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And as for him being a commander of the military in the Knin area, was that because you had any information or was it because it's a guess?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was my conclusion. General Cermak was the highest ranking officer that we worked with, in terms of coordinating with the army. I believe no one outranked him in the area. This was a logical conclusion that I draw intuitively, you might say, but I did not see any documents to that effect, and that is about as much as I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So would it be fair to say, then, that it's because of his rank that you make these statements of opinion, rather than knowing what his function was?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: The witness has given an answer that's based upon his experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Which is why there then -- what's just put to him, I take it that that's what you'd like it raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes. I think it would be more fair to -- to -- acknowledge that -- those aspects of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There's nothing wrong with the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, of course, there's a -- I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, in my submission there is nothing wrong with the question at all. And in fact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, there's nothing wrong with the question. Nevertheless, if it -- whether it gives the -- certainly in cross-examination you can put to a witness something he has not yet said, that, as such -- not wrong. At the same time, I wonder whether it gives us always the best evidence available. Mr. Buhin, you said General Cermak was the highest ranking officer that you worked with, in terms of coordinating with the army. Now, was it just because he was a general; or was it also on the type of work he was involved that you concluded that he was the commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Most probably because we cooperated with him and he was a general by rank. It was only a lengthy period after I had returned from Knin that I found out that General Gotovina had been there as well. General Zagorac was also referred to. During my stay in Knin I had never heard of those persons in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were there areas, according to your knowledge, for which General Cermak was not competent to deal, was it limited to certain areas? You mentioned the coordination between civilians and the army. Were there -- did you learn anything about the activities in which he was involved, being, as you said, the highest ranking person you were aware of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As regards his other activities and his participation in dealing with other problems, I cannot say anything about that. I know that he was in charge of coordination, that there were coordination meetings, in fact, at General Cermak's office; but to what an extent he participated in resolving other problems, I don't know. I know that we informed him and submitted to him reports on the work of the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kay, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just looking that other matter. When you say, "I know we informed him and submitted to him reports on the work of the police," first of all, you're not talking about written reports. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. We would inform him orally. Rather, colleague Baric and colleague Cedo Romanic would report on problems, would inform about problems that we were encountering and about the planned activity of the police and what the police was to do. In some instances we sought cooperation with the military police. We pointed out problems, problems associated with people in military uniform freely moving about.
