So, in principle, at such meetings, we informed him of what we had learned and about what we -- and told him what we thought should be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And that information was being given to him because he was coordinating other agencies in the area. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The practice was for us to cooperate closely with him and to inform him of things. He probably required such information in order to be able to coordinate with other agencies in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. You said quite clearly yesterday that Mr. Cermak could not command you in the police. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Because you're in a separate hierarchy from the military. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. We received orders directly from the Ministry of the Interior. We complied with them in accordance with our powers, and wherever there was something controversial, we always sought the approval and consent of the minister of the interior. We could not get any orders from the army directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And what was happening was that information was being given to General Cermak by the civilian police. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: From our side, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And at the meetings, you would see if there was information from other agencies who required the help of the fundamental police. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, could we learn what meetings you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm referring to the meetings at General Cermak's office, Your Honour. I haven't diverted from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which were not attended by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, he was asked about it in chief, so I've been dealing with it this way, Your Honour. The Prosecution asked about it so I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry, I will repeat -- to be fair to you, I'll repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You asked the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: My eyes are not so good as they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- what was happening was that information was being given to General Cermak by the civilian police. Is that right? And then -- let me just see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think there's something missing on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see that the meetings are missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: It refers to a technical difficulty at 54, 22.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see that. Page 54, line 22. That's just before my intervention, Mr. Kay, there was a technical difficulty. Perhaps you try to catch up from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: My eyes weren't as bad as I thought they were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- because I couldn't see it. Now I know the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And to be fair, you didn't go to the meeting so you don't know what was discussed. Is that right, Mr. Buhin?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not entirely sure that the -- that's a logical conclusion. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I don't think that you have to be concerned about that, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You asked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- in view of the question Mr. Kay did put, he is certainly not seeking the witness to say, No, I have got no idea what happened there. That's for -- because I wasn't present. The reason I intervened, Mr. Kay, is because you used, although I can't read it anymore, what you observed in the meetings. That's the reason why I intervened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's leave it to Mr. Kay for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And I was trying to follow, Your Honour, to assist on that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is clear and Mr. Margetts assisted us --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: He didn't object against Your Honour but he did --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He wisely did not. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Buhin, back, then, to business. At the meetings that were held at the offices of General Cermak, just so we establish this, you've told us you weren't present, and so we're right to say you don't know what was actually said. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: After these meetings were held, we would talk about it. In the police station -- in the police administration so that I was informed about the substance of the meetings by colleagues who had attended the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Very right, and that's a very good answer. And that's what I want to ask you about. Was it clear to you from how they spoke to you, that at those meetings they were told to do their job of policing?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they had to be told that. We knew what we were to do and we merely informed the General about what was going on and what we were doing about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And would your colleagues come back and report problems that other agencies were talking about in the meetings?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it touched upon work, police work, we would discuss that too. What was not of the essence for the work of the police would not be related to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: For instance, if I give an example and tell me if it's a wrong example, civilians coming into the region who had previously lived there and were looking to get back to their properties and homes. Was that a problem that was discussed after a meeting between you, Mr. Baric, Mr. Romanic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Definitely must have been a problem, because there was a procedure in place for registering those persons who were found there after Operation Oluja as well as of persons who arrived in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And this caused a big problem that the police had to deal with, because the number of people coming into the region was expanding by each day.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was a problem, because very soon after our own arrival, a large number of civilians started flocking in and they were hard to keep tabs on, and that was an extra effort on our part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, could we try to become a bit more concrete so as if you say, was that a problem, what I'd like to know from the witness is if this was discussed, what did this result in, what did you, as a police officer, or a police force, what did you do about the newly coming in -- what were your activities in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I was going to actually take it in stages, identify what the problem was and then what they --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do see. But if we get a broad description of many, many problems, of course, if it is obvious that people coming in may have created a problem, then we could more quickly go to -- to come to the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Such as if the witness tells us that they raise the issue of people in uniforms freely moving around, apparently a matter which was raised with Mr. Cermak, then what I'd like to know is what was the result of having raised this. Did you -- what was the result of any coordinating activity, what did you do about people in uniform freely moving around, just as to what extent did you adapt your work to the people coming in newly? What -- what concrete steps, what concrete activity, or what change in your activity was the result of what was discussed during these meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In respect of the free movement of persons in military uniform, it was practically impossible for us to take any measures. The General informed us that we should be patient and that units of the Croatian army would be withdrawing from Knin very shortly. The few people that would remain would be easier to deal with by the police. And that was so indeed. But the problem that we had was that a large number of civilians had arrived over a very short period of time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That comes then to the second point. You said about the people in uniform freely moving around almost nothing or nothing could be done. Now you come to the other point. Mr. Kay, if you want to take it in small steps. But let me say the following. If we want to move forward, you can take too big steps and can you also take many, many very small steps, which certainly slows down the way in which you proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I don't want to frustrate the Court with this, but there are a number of different issues in relation to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you can find a fair balance between proceeding and not taking too big steps but also not too small steps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Had it been expected that a large number of civilians would come into the area as soon as they did?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We were taken by surprise because it had not been announced. After the arrival of the train and the establishment of regular services, a large number of civilians came and we had difficulty receiving all of them. People's papers needed to be checked, people went to see their flats, their facilities, their houses. People had to be able to prove that the things they had taken were indeed theirs, and these were the kinds of problems that the civilian police had to grapple with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Are you able to say where these civilians were coming from?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: From all over Croatia where they had gone to as exiles. They were in the areas of Split, Sibenik, Zadar, in the continental part of Croatia -- almost in the entire continental part of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And as the MUP, were you able to stop them coming in?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This was an order that came from the top, I'm not sure whether from the government or the Presidency of Croatia, that was transmitted to the Ministry of Interior that they should be able to pass through with passes and being registered, but later, this practice was abolished so that they could come without having to produce any passes. And then there were persons who came into the area just out of curiosity, to see what it looked like.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You referred yesterday to the train and the president coming to Knin on the train. Were you aware if the train from Split to Zagreb was actually running into Knin before the president came on the freedom train?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the train. I don't know that the train passed there before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that might be a convenient moment. If I check whether I've got any more cross-examination to do, I've finished earlier, if I have; or I will certainly finish earlier if I have a bit more to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll leave you some time to consider that. We'll have a break, and we'll resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay. Oh, we have no witness yet. Could the witness be brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, to let the Court know, I have finished my questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Number two was you, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will be the number two, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Buhin, Mr. Kay informed us that he has finished his questioning. You will now be cross-examined by Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Mikulicic is counsel for Mr. Markac. Mr. Mikulicic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Buhin.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will be asking you some questions on behalf of General Markac's Defence. Before we begin, I will ask you to please bear in mind the fact that whatever we are saying is being interpreted for the benefit of the court record. Therefore, please pause after each of my questions before you start your answer and I will do the same, which will allow us to give the interpreters a chance to do their job properly.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buhin, you have been with the police for a long time. How long was your career with the police?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: 20 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You consider yourself an experienced police officer, right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, I do.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, could Mr. Mikulicic please speak a little closer to the microphone because we can't hear him properly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you speak closer to the microphone, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will try to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the eve of Operation Storm, you were with the Ministry of Interior. Which department?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Uniformed police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: At the time, were you with the prevention unit of the uniformed police?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have D527 brought up. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buhin, we are about to see the decree on the internal structure and modus operandi of the Ministry of Interior of the Republic of Croatia. This is already an exhibit in this trial. This decree talks about how the MUP is organised. If we move on to page 4, we see that the decree talks about the police sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 4, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We have the police department within the police sector; that is Article 10. And within the police department, we have two sections, the prevention section and the security section. That's on the next page. But we will not be needing this for the time being. You told us that you were with the prevention section. Just to remind you, may I put it to you that this section's job was to make proposals and take measures to train police and also to make proposals for measures and provide any technical assistance as well as supervise work done in various police administrations. These are the legal foundations and the result of these -- one of the results is the role of coordinator. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The role of coordinator is a peculiar one within the Ministry of Interior. This isn't something that is envisaged by this decree. Is that not a fact, sir?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This role, in a way, was something that was agreed within the ministry because of the newly arisen situation in the liberated area. What was required was to find a way to set up the police bodies in the area, right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I believe that this was the practical solution for that problem at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Prior to Operation Storm, the role of coordinator was envisaged in Knin in a certain way, but prior to Operation Storm that never existed, did it, that role?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true. This was the first time I came across anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... pause now and then. May I remind to you do the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm sorry. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We've heard already about the way in which it worked and what your principle task was. It was to help uniformed police, right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But you had nothing do with the crime police, did you?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The need for a coordinator, this -- this is a newly liberated area and one had to set up a police administration as well as police stations within the existing framework. You agree with me, right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When you came there, you found a chief of the police administration there and that was Mr. Romanic, right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'm looking at your statement, P963, paragraph 12. You say that Mr. Romanic was a very professional police officer. You believe that Serbs were appointed to certain positions within the police for political motives, but you couldn't tell which political motives precisely. Let us say a thing or two about that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 65 ter 3143.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buhin, what we're about to look at is the constitutional Law on Human Rights and Freedoms and the Rights of Ethnic Minorities in the Republic of Croatia. The Trial Chamber is aware of the fact that in Croatia's territory there was a substantial Serb ethnic minority. Under the constitution, they had certain rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have Article 19 of the constitutional law displayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This is about proportional representation in bodies of government and this is it about the representatives of various ethnic minorities. Can you please look at Article 19, Mr. Buhin, it reads: "Members of ethnic national communities or minorities have the right to be represented in the bodies of local self-government in proportion to their share in the overall population of the respective local self-government unit." Now that I have shown you this law, this constitutional law, do you agree with me that the matter of appointing a chief of police administration in an area that, according to the census, was predominantly Serb is a move that is politically clever but it is also based on the constitutional law and it follows from this constitutional law?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm entirely in agreement with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have a number for this 65 ter document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D836.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D836 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Mikulicic, you were referring to paragraph 12 of the -- of P963. As it appears in e-court, it is without numbering of paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes. That will be in the -- in the Croatian version that will be paragraph one, two, three, four, on page 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Just so that we save other people from counting all the paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I did it by myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In English it is page 3, the fourth paragraph. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, when you arrived in Knin, you met the newly appointed chief of the police administration, and the commander of the police station, Mr. Mihic, right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Romanic and Mr. Mihic. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You describe the situation that you found when you came, there no electricity, no telephone, it was difficult, and so on and so forth. Nevertheless, would you agree -- you said there was a shortage of police officers. Was this not also a consequence of the fact that many experienced Serb police officers, if I may put it that way, during the existence of the Republic of Serbian Krajina changed sides, thereby abandoning their positions within the Croatian police or the Croatian Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is certainly true, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: One had to make up for all those absences, not just in terms of numbers but also in terms of professional skill and ability, right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One tried to compensate for that, but there were a lot of policemen who hadn't even completed their elementary schooling, and the courses they followed or the training programmes were sometimes no longer than two months which was fairly insufficient to qualify them for police work, but that was what the situation dictated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: At the time, Mr. Buhin, did you have the following experience. The Ministry of Interior, in terms how it was structured, was at the very centre, and it did what it could to bring manning levels up in these police administrations across the newly liberated areas. They did what they could and that also entailed your role of coordinator, did it not?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The ministry did what it could at the time, what it could reasonably be expected to do, under the circumstances, and this entailed all the police administrations and police stations across Croatia. Men were seconded, to the extent possible, without jeopardizing or compromising the work of local police in the areas from which men were being seconded to the newly liberated areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You, the coordinators, were, in a manner of speaking, a tool employed by this policy. The policy being to get the greatest possible assistance to these local police stations and units that were being set up. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And this was probably the only course of action open to us at the time because the newly appointed chief of the police administration and the commander of the police station had little or no experience in leadership, and they knew little or nothing about how to run a police administration or a police station. They were to some extent experienced police officers but they needed assistance in terms of organizing all these things and setting them up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You also testified that there was another problem. Some of the police officers seconded from other areas across Croatia were not entirely familiar with the area, with the lie of the land. However, you also say that a lot of the ground was booby-trapped. Therefore, it was dangerous to leave any of the main roads and take any of the village roads leading to villages in that mountainous area. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All of that is entirely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buhin, what about these booby-trapped areas?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Mikulicic, listening to your question, I made some comments when Mr. Kay cross-examined the witness. I said small steps, big steps. It seems that you are taking rather big steps. And also I asked him to focus on what we -- what was done concretely. Now if I listen to your last question, that reflects almost literally what the witness said about the reasons why, in the Grubori incident, the people that were sent caused them not to be able to find it, unfamiliar with the area -- everything is more or less repetition. Now, is there any reason to deal with that in a general way, where it has been explained in the very concrete circumstances of people being sent to Grubori. And that question came to my mind several times. Is there any need to give the big picture -- of course, I'm not saying that background and environment is -- is not of some importance. But of primary importance is what the witness observed, what he saw, what he heard, what he did, et cetera, of course in the context of the totality. And where I invited Mr. Kay to find a balance, I would like to invite you also to find a balance between what is background, general information, and what is concrete, not knowledge of this witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. I will move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We mentioned the areas that were booby-trapped. The mines needed clearing and this was something that was done by specially trained units, right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: On the part of the Ministry of Interior, we are talking about special police units. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think not. There were areas that were booby-trapped, areas that we were informed about as being booby-trapped, and these areas were cleared by special civil protection units. There was a special team in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Talking about special police, it is not the houses, the buildings there that I had in mind. I meant the ground covered and searched by the special police while tracking down any remaining enemies and then there were mines that were laid there and booby-traps and so on and so forth. So that was one of the tasks of the special police?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. That was one of their tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'm about to show you a document that is already an exhibit. This is D399. This is a document produced by the chief of the -- military police administration, Mr. Lausic, and we are going straight to page 2. It reads: "In addition to combat activity, members of the special police also were responsible for searching the area." The Chamber knows about other documents that talk about this as well. It's D293. And then the next document would be D399, as well as D506, and D554. Further, D559, and so on and so forth. All these documents show that the military police with its own units, to a large extent, was involved in clearing and searching the terrain. Mr. Buhin, if we look at this order that is on our screens right now, if we go to the last page of that order, we shall see that it was not delivered to the Ministry of Interior, which means that you were not informed about this. Is that the reason that you were unfamiliar, as you said, with the fact that members of the military police, too, were involved in searching and clearing the ground?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the conclusion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Conclusion, Mr. Mikulicic, what you said, it's not addressed to this unit or person or institution. So therefore you have not seen it. That's a conclusion which is not for you to draw. If there's a chance that the witness may have seen, you could ask him and otherwise you just say this is a document addressed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I was trying to make a big step, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes. And also, Mr. President, I think the suggestion was a little bit broader than that. It was referring to the subject matter suggesting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that Mr. Mikulicic will now take some smaller steps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Buhin, can you please go to the very last page of this order, or, rather, this report. If I look at my copy, I see at least who it was delivered to. But, all right, we can go on and use a different copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 03242, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'm about to show you another order of the military police administration. The chief, Mate Lausic, if you look at Article 2 you will see that anti-terror platoons and other members of the military police - and it's the 9th of August, 1995, that we are talking about - these people are involved in combat. They need to be rested, and then they need to be sent out to search and clear these newly liberated areas of the Republic of Croatia. My question to you, sir, is have you ever seen an order like this?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This order was sent to the military police; but we do not see it being sent, at the very least, to the attention of the Ministry of Interior. If we go to page 2 of this order, we see that it was delivered to the defence minister, to the chief of the Main Staff, to the assistant minister for security, and to a number of commanders. Therefore, no Ministry of Interior. I am putting it to you that your ignorance of the fact that the military police was involved searching the ground is a result of the fact that you were not among the addressees and did not receive any of their orders. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have a number for 03242 ter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit number D837, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D837 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buhin, we've been looking at some orders to do with the military police. I'm about to show you a different order, and this is D559. This is an order by the chief of Croatian army's Main Staff, General Zvonimir Cervenko. The date is the 14th of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... but I'd -- yes, now. Mr. Mikulicic, let me try to understand the evidence you're eliciting from this witness. You asked him about the tasks of the special police - I'm referring to page 69 - what their tasks were and you said tracking down remaining enemies and there were mines that were laid and booby-traps and so on. So you gave -- and then the witness confirmed that that was the task of the special police. Now, in relation to the last document, you said: "I'm putting to you that your ignorance of the fact that" -- oh, that was the military police here. I'm sorry, I made a mistake, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I now understand your testimony which I did not --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: -- what I'm trying to do is to show up that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's clear you are making --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: -- besides the special police, there were others who were also performing the mop-up operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's clear to me now. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In respect of what you see, I shall first ask you, Mr. Buhin, did you ever have occasion to see the order of the chief of the Main Staff of the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Look at first -- at B on the first page, what the Chief of Staff is ordering. He says: "Reserve forces, namely, Home Guard and domicile units as well as intervention guard units, should be used to search the terrain and mop up areas from any remaining or possibly infiltrated enemy bands in an organised, planned and consecutive fashion." You told us that you personally have not seen this order or anything similar, and I should like to refer you to page 5 of the same order, which shows that this order was not submitted to anybody within the Ministry of Interior. Mr. Buhin, having seen these documents, do you agree that some other units, other than special police units, also participated in the searching and mopping up of the terrain during and immediately after Operation Oluja?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm not entirely sure that the witness has had an opportunity to see these documents. We're moving very fast. The witness has given a lot of evidence about certain things that he may not have received that certain discussions that people he was associated with may have had, so if we want to explore the witness's knowledge about these topics, I suggest we do so properly. If the witness's evidence on these matters is not so relevant, then I'm not entirely sure about the use of putting these documents to him at this pace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think there are two issues, Mr. Mikulicic. The one is what is the knowledge of this witness about tasks for the military police in mopping up operations; that's one. And the second, the witness told us that he was not aware of that. The second issue, then, is whether these documents are evidence that they were. The witness may not be able to tell us anything about it. It may be a matter of drawing conclusions. If the witness says, I've not thoroughly studied this but that is the conclusion of these documents, then that is it a matter that is not a knowledge of facts that the witness observed. I do understand that you would like to tender these documents as evidence that what the witness did not know -- at least on the basis of the documents, is probable or you may even consider it to be proven. I leave that to you what conclusions to draw out of that. But to ask the witness documents of five pages which he hasn't -- which he has not studied, to say whether this rebuts what he did not know to be the case, that might not be a very good way of proceeding. This is not in any way to stop you to present this evidence but just to make a clear distinction between what the witness can tell us and what you invite the Chamber to conclude on the basis of documents you're presenting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'll move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let's move on to another topic. It is about civilian protection. What information did you have during the time you were in Knin as a coordinator about the role and task of the civilian protection? Did you have any contacts with them, with representatives of the civilian protection?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had contacts with them on a daily basis. They would inform us of where they would go, which areas they would go to in order to de-mine them, and they asked for our assistance there, to provide the necessary security. And we know that they also cleared up, cleaned flats, streets, different premises, and they encountered a multitude of problems because they didn't have the necessary equipment, the necessary vehicles, and they operated under very difficult conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you recall what were the civilian protection members wearing? Did they have any kind of uniform? What were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot describe their uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said, Mr. Buhin, that their task was to enter flats and houses that had been abandoned by the departing Serbian population from that area. What was it that they were supposed to look for and establish in such houses and flats?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The greater problems were the refrigerators that were left loaded with meat because, due to combat operations, the electricity was down and there would be no electricity for five or ten days. So the meat in them rotted and there were maggots actually emerging from the refrigerators. As far as we knew, this threatened with large-scale epidemic, and that is one of the tasks that they had to carry out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Will you tell us, you said a while ago that they were poorly equipped. What vehicles did the civilian protection member use when they took away such objects from the abandoned houses and flats?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, they had a small number of very few trucks, i.e., freight vehicles. In most cases, they would exactly habilitate the vehicles which they had found in the liberated area to suit their particular purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to civilian vehicles?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Any vehicles, all vehicles that they found and that they could put to some use.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned as one of the duties of the civilian protection members being the locating of explosives. They had a crime scene examiner, a forensic technician on the team, did they not, and he was equipped for that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had a de-mining team as part of the civilian protection team and they were trained to find and defuse mines. The crime scene examiner or forensic technician actually was used to process and -- and sanitize areas where the corpse were found.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What are you actually saying? What was their particular role? What was their task -- what was his task, that of the forensic technician, that is. Do you know anything specific?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know the details. I can only assume that as a crime person he was able to register or to establish in what way, more or less, the person in question had met his death.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In your recollection, did the civilian protection team actually find explosives and weapons in flats and houses and similar objects?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember any such instances.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let us move on to another topic and that is a topic that has been discussed at some length. That is, the topic of Grubori. This Chamber has heard quite a few testimonies and been presented a lot of evidence on this topic, but what I would like to know is this: What was the task of the uniformed police, when a report -- when the report was received in police station Knin that some bodies had been found in Grubori? What was the primary task of the uniformed police, in your professional opinion?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As in any such -- other such instance, the primary task was to attend the scene, verify the information received, and if indeed bodies were found, to secure the scene of the event until the arrival of the expert team of forensic people of the crime police or the investigating judge together with the crime police team.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What does that mean to provide security, to secure the scene, in your view?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To secure the scene so as to retain it in the state as found, in order to prevent any changes from occurring at the scene until the expert team arrives.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We know from previous testimonies given before this Court that at the -- it was the UN members who arrived first at the scene in Grubori and that it was them, actually, who photographed the scene, entered the premises, registered the situation at the scene, talked to the locals, et cetera. Talking from the police standpoint, is that an appropriate procedure in terms of securing the scene of the event?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At any rate, after such information is received, our task is to go to the scene of the event and secure what we find at the moment we get there. Any changes that have occurred before that or after that is something that would be ascertained later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You told us that the -- the uniformed police patrol did not find the place and that they returned, that they came back. After that, what was the task of the uniformed police at the police station in Knin, of the operations duty service, after they received the report about the finding of these bodies at that scene? Did they have to inform anybody about that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We, in the administration were informed about it, the chief of the police administration, the coordinators as well. I do not remember how -- whether it was possible to coordinate -- communicate with the police administration in Zadar at that time. But the first task which was carried out was to inform the police administration, namely, Mr. Cedo Romanic, was aware of it, we knew of it, and we agreed further on how to proceed in our task.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was it the obligation of the operative duty service of the Knin police station to inform the operative duty service of the police administration in Zadar?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that it was at that time, because this station was actually part of the police administration in Knin, and the operation duty service did not have -- it did not have a specific separate operation duty service but we functioned as a staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do I understand you correctly: At that time, the police administration of the district of Knin was supposed to inform the operative duty service in Zadar, right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you personally know that that did happen; namely, that the operative duty service of the Zadar police administration was indeed informed about the incident at Grubori?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot be sure of that, but I am sure that Mr. Ivo Cetina, as chief of the police administration, was directly informed, and it was his task to refer it further to his administration, to his operations duty service, and to take the necessary further measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You told us that you had personally talked to Mr. Cetina about the incident in Grubori and that you had reported to him about it. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you inform, so to speak, your superior coordinator, Mr. Franjo, about that incident?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And then Mr. Cetina told you that he required some time but that he would ensure an on-site investigation team, and you expected an on-site investigation team to come, right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the way in which an investigating judge who is competent over an area is informed to perform an investigation?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In practice and in normal circumstances, the police administration operations duty service informs the investigating judge of any event which requires the attendance at the scene of the crime police. And it is the decision of the investigating judge whether he will attend the scene himself or leave that task to members of the crime police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buhin, do you know that in this specific case, the one in Grubori, whether the investigating judge had been indeed informed?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I believe that Mr. Cetina had done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You believed because that is standard procedure. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had promised that he would do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Kardum? He was the chief of the crime police department in the police administration of Zadar.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I met him in the police administration, but I do not remember whether it was in those days, when I came to the police administration before departing for Knin, or in an encounter during my stay in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: As chief of the crime police in the crime -- in the police administration, Mr. Kardum was the person who was supposed to form the crime police team to take part in the on-site investigation with the investigating judge. Is that not so?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He should have done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That means that Mr. Kardum should have been informed about the event in Grubori in order to be able to set up a team of forensic experts.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he should have been. That is quite logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum testified before this Court. That is page 9361, line 18 of the transcript, and he said that he had not at all been informed about the incident at Grubori. I know you don't know yourself why that is the case but perhaps you can tell us this. Was this something that was only to be expected, as far as a regular procedure was concerned whenever a suspicious incident was being reported?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Normally, he would have been among the first to know. However, the circumstances being what they were, a lot of shortcuts were taken and corners were cut.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: May I ask you this: Do you perhaps know why Mr. Kardum was not informed?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You refer to Mr. Sacic in your evidence, who arrived in Knin about the Grubori the incident. What was his role within the police structure and organisation?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he was the deputy chief of the special police units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Given what you tell us about his role or position, let's talk about him in relation to the uniformed police. Does he have any powers over the uniformed police, in terms of giving orders or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buhin, did he have any powers over you, in terms of giving orders?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, none.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Now I draw your attention to a portion in your statement. This is page 4, paragraph 3, from the bottom of the page up. You state: "When I spoke to Sacic, he said that any murders would be handled as a by-product of Operation Storm. It struck me as strange that he should say that. It also struck me as strange that he had come to Knin. My own view is Sacic tried to cover the murders, but I have no idea why." Of course, I know that it has been a long time and many of these developments have since failed in your memory. Do try to remember, however, why did you form this opinion; namely, that Sacic was out to conceal the murders, to hush them up? When you ponder the same thing today, is your opinion or your impression still the same as it was back then?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my first impression. If I ask myself the same question today, Sacic would have been wrong in trying to conceal or hush up those murders. That was my first impression on account of the altercation that occurred and also because Mr. Moric had called to say that I should mind my own business and not meddle in anyone else's. That was my first impression and it was a somewhat weird impression, so for a while I went on believing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In a way, you felt hurt by this, if my understanding is correct, right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: On the one hand, you were trying to help; on the other, your own superiors simply instructed you to mind your own business and this had to do with the uniformed police and not interfere with the business of the crime police. Would that be an accurate conclusion?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very much so. All the more given the fact, as we all knew, that the UN police had been to the scene by this time. They were perfectly well trained and they knew how to do their work. Therefore, it would have been entirely impractical to go and try and cover up something like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buhin, you are an experienced police officer and you know the ins and outs of your line of work. The first duty of any police officer is to observe the law, right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Quite so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: However, what would a policeman do in the following hypothetical situation. His superior gives him an order that is illegal or not in keeping with the laws. You have over 20 years' experience working with the police. How do you see this situation?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I would have the responsibility of pointing this out to my superior, that his order is illegitimate or illegal. Secondly, if there was the slightest chance that I would harm anyone in the exercise of this order, I would have to desist and refuse to obey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is my conclusion right, if I suggested this. If a policeman agrees to carry out such an order, he is in breach of the law himself, despite the fact that this is an order that is issued to him by his superior?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is entirely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buhin, did you ever receive from anyone any order at all to do something that you were not bound to do by the law or, alternatively, to perform an action that was illegal? Did you ever find yourself on the receiving end of an order like that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember any specific incident involving something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Again, hypothetically, and I do have a high regard for your experience and professionalism, try to imagine yourself in a situation where a superior comes up to you and gives you an order that you deem is illegal. What would you do?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, the same as any other police officer. I would draw my superior's intention to the illegal nature of the whole procedure, and I would refuse to obey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so am I.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I would like to pass on the other theme, but I don't think it is appropriate to commence with a few questions and then stop until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time would you still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I think I will be finished within 20 minutes, or 30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Which you -- would keep you exactly within the time-limits you -- if it would be 30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber would grant you, also in view of the way in which the time was used, another 20 minutes tomorrow, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if you leave out some of the hypothetical questions, then you might have saved already the ten minutes you might be short of. Then, Mr. Buhin, we'll adjourn for the day. We'd like to see you back tomorrow, although we first will hear briefly another witness, that means -- which means that we will not start at a quarter past 2.00 further hearing your evidence, but only later that afternoon. Most likely that will be approximately at -- a little bit after 4.00. I would like to remind you that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony, whether already given or still to be given, and we'd like to see you back at a bit of an uncertain time tomorrow, later in the afternoon. We adjourn, and we will resume tomorrow, the 8th of October, quarter past 2.00 in this courtroom, III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
